On 15 January 2026, Goa Police deployed a vehicle-mounted signal jammer at Merces junction during the Chimbel villagers’ protest against the Unity Mall project. Journalists covering the Dhadak Morcha reported live broadcasts and mobile networks were blocked. Media confronted DIG Varsha Sharma on camera. She asked for time to check. The jammer was switched off only after reports went public.
Facts on record:

•  The Rs 4.9 crore jammer vehicle was flagged off in December 2025 by CM Pramod Sawant as a VVIP/IED security asset, not as a tool to stop press coverage of a public protest.
•  St Andre MLA Viresh Borkar raised the issue in the Assembly. The CM said he would look into it.
•  Eight months later, no officer has been named as the authorising authority and no inquiry outcome has been made public.
Why this is not a routine “law and order” step:

Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution protects freedom of speech and expression, which the Supreme Court has held includes press freedom and the right to receive and impart information. Article 19(1)(b) protects peaceful assembly. Restrictions are allowed only on the narrow grounds in Article 19(2) and must be reasonable.

In Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court held that cutting communications is a drastic restriction on Article 19. It must be necessary, proportionate, the least intrusive option, and backed by a published, reasoned order that can be challenged in court. No such published order for this jammer deployment has been produced.

The Department of Telecommunications has stated that signal jammers are generally illegal for unauthorised use. Possession and use require specific government licence. Using a VVIP-security jammer to black out journalists at a village protest is not the purpose for which the vehicle was publicly justified.
Blocking live reporting of a protest does not only affect cameras. It prevents citizens from seeing how the State treats people who dissent. That is the opposite of transparency.

Questions that still have no answer:
1.  Who authorised the jammer at Merces on 15 January 2026 — DIG, DGP, Home Department, or political executive?
2.  Was there a written order? If yes, produce it.
3.  Why was a device meant for VVIP/IED protection used against the press?
4.  Why has nobody been held accountable after the CM said he would look into it?

Freedom of the press is not a favour from the ruling party. It is a constitutional right. If this deployment was lawful, publish the order. If it was not, name the officer and the minister who will take responsibility.

Mobile internet was cut in parts of central Delhi as thousands of students marched on parliament. Here is what makes it worse than a routine shutdown. No suspension order has been published by anyone, which breaks India's own Supreme Court ruling and two of its own laws requiring published, written reasons. So the network goes dark exactly when people are protesting, and the government does not even follow its own process for doing it. India recorded 65 shutdowns in 2025, the most of any democracy on earth. A blackout during a protest, with no order and no reasons, is not security. It is a government switching off the witnesses.
#InternetFreedom #DigitalRights

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

UPSC Mains | Core Facts, Arguments & Insights:- 
Central Thesis: Internet Shutdowns are an extraordinary legal measure, permissible only under strict constitutional, statutory, and judicial safeguards, not as a routine administrative response.

Legal Framework: Internet suspension is governed by the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, replacing the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885 and 2017 Rules.

Permissible Grounds: Shutdowns are allowed only in cases of Public Emergency or Public Safety, supported by written reasons, competent authority approval, and defined objectives.

Doctrine of Proportionality: Authorities must adopt the Least Restrictive Measure; blanket internet suspension should be the last resort, not the first response.

Supreme Court Doctrine: In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court held that internet access is intrinsically linked to Article 19(1)(a) (Freedom of Speech & Expression) and Article 19(1)(g) (Freedom of Trade & Profession).

Judicial Safeguards: Every shutdown order must be Reasoned, Time-Bound, Published, Subject to Review, and Open to Judicial Scrutiny; Indefinite Shutdowns are Unconstitutional.

Implementation Concern: Despite the new legal regime, some States reportedly continue relying on outdated legal provisions, raising concerns over procedural compliance and rule of law.

Global Position: India continues to record one of the world's highest numbers of internet shutdowns, making digital governance and rights protection key policy concerns.

Democratic Impact: Internet shutdowns affect Freedom of Expression, Digital Economy, Education, Emergency Services, Business Continuity, and Citizen Access to Information.

Policy Imperative: Strengthen Legal Accountability, Transparent Decision-Making, Periodic Review, Targeted Restrictions, and Digital Rights Protection while preserving Public Order.

Author's Core Argument

> Internet shutdowns must remain an exceptional, legally proportionate, and judicially reviewable instrument. Democratic governance requires balancing legitimate security concerns with constitutional freedoms, ensuring that digital rights are not curtailed through excessive executive discretion.

🚨 VPN BAN ENFORCED ACROSS DODA DISTRICT AMID SECURITY CONCERNS.

DODA, INDIA - Authorities in Jammu and Kashmir have imposed a two‑month ban on virtual private networks across Doda district, citing concerns over encrypted traffic being used to bypass cyber restrictions and access prohibited online content. The order, issued by District Magistrate Krishan Lal under provisions of recent security legislation, directs all internet service providers to block VPN usage and warns individuals and businesses against attempts to circumvent the restrictions.

Officials say the move follows reports that certain groups were using VPNs to access banned applications and coordinate activities that could threaten public order. The ban applies to residents, institutions, cyber cafés and commercial entities, with exceptions only for government‑authorised use. Enforcement has been handed to local police, who are expected to monitor compliance throughout the 60‑day period.

The district has seen periodic digital controls in recent years, often tied to heightened vigilance in sensitive areas. The latest order notes that misuse of encrypted channels poses risks ranging from dissemination of inflammatory material to coordination of unlawful activity. A review of the restrictions is expected once the two‑month window ends.

Saying "never buy a Bravia" is an opinion. Saying "Sony sold us a warranty then refused it"—while deliberately hiding that the screen was physically smashed—is a misleading factual claim. A Cease and Desist is a pre-litigation demand, not a filed lawsuit or court verdict. The bench asked the Collector's advocate to clarify whether the order would be withdrawn, warning that appropriate judicial action would follow if it wasn't. • The video contains statements found to insult Bhagwan Shri Ram, Bhagwan Shri Krishna, and Sita Devi.
• It was found to make claims that they consumed meat and alcohol using disputed interpretations of scriptures.
• The GAC held that the content hurts the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus and is contrary to societal harmony.
• YouTube's free speech arguments were not accepted, with the order noting that freedom of expression is subject to the reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

The order follows the Hon'ble Delhi High Court's direction dated 3 July 2026 requiring the appeal to be decided within 15 days.

The complainant has also stated that these findings may be relevant to a separate pending petition before a Magistrate seeking registration of an FIR against Dhruv Rathee, which is listed for hearing on 10 September 2026.

🚨⚖️🏛️ BREAKING GSTAT RULING: GSTR-2A vs GSTR-3B MISMATCH ALONE CANNOT JUSTIFY DENIAL OF ITC! 🏛️⚖️🚨
⚖️ GSTAT Bengaluru | M/s Peekay Industries v. Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, Karnataka | Order dated 03.09.2026

🔥 Major ruling on ITC mismatch disputes: GSTAT Bengaluru has held that a difference between GSTR-2A and GSTR-3B may justify verification, but cannot, by itself, be treated as conclusive proof of wrongful ITC availment.

🔍📑 The Tribunal observed that mismatch is only the beginning of an enquiry, not its end. Any demand must be based on proper examination of records and the taxpayer's explanation.

💡📊 For FY 2019-20, GSTAT noted that Section 16(2)(aa) was not applicable, having come into force only from 01.01.2022. It further observed that GSTR-2A during the relevant period was a facilitative, auto-populated statement without independent statutory force as a condition for ITC. Rule 36(4) itself came into force only from 09.10.2019.

🚫⚖️ The Tribunal also flagged a serious Section 75(7) issue: while the SCN proposed liability under IGST, the final order confirmed demand under CGST and SGST. A demand cannot travel beyond the amount, heads or grounds specified in the SCN.

📚🔎 GSTAT directed invoice-wise and, wherever necessary, supplier-wise verification, including examination of invoices, purchase register, books and electronic credit ledger. Before drawing an adverse inference from a GSTR-2A shortfall, the authority must also examine the compliance status of concerned suppliers.

⚡ RESULT: Both the original adjudication order and first appellate order were SET ASIDE and the matter remanded for fresh adjudication, strictly confined to the original SCN — no expansion or enhancement of demand permitted. 🛡️⚖️

📌 BIG TAKEAWAY:
GSTR-2A mismatch ≠ automatic ITC denial. 🔍 Actual verification + evidence + proper SCN + speaking order are essential before ITC can be denied. ⚖️📑✅

🚨⚖️🏛️ BREAKING: SUPREME COURT REFUSES TO REVIVE ₹363 CRORE GST DEMAND AGAINST VODAFONE IDEA — PROCEEDINGS AGAINST NON-EXISTENT COMPANY CANNOT STAND 🏛️⚖️🚨

📅 07 September 2026 | Supreme Court of India

⚖️ The Supreme Court has dismissed the Centre’s appeal seeking revival of a massive ₹363 crore GST demand arising from proceedings initiated against Vodafone Mobile Services Ltd. (VMSL), an entity that had already ceased to exist pursuant to amalgamation. A Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and N. Vinod Chandran upheld the Bombay High Court’s decision quashing the proceedings.

🔹 🏢 Non-existent entity: VMSL had merged with Vodafone India Ltd. and Idea Cellular Ltd. pursuant to an NCLT order in August 2018, whereas DGGI issued the show-cause notice to VMSL only in August 2024. The Supreme Court questioned how proceedings could be initiated against a company that had already ceased to exist.

🔹 💰 ₹363 crore dispute: The demand related to the 2017 transfer of VMSL’s telecom tower business to ATC Telecom Infrastructure as a going concern on slump-sale basis. The Department alleged that the transfer was an exempt supply and consequently disputed the ITC claimed.

🔹 📜 Section 87 argument rejected: The Department relied upon Section 87 of the CGST Act to contend that pre-merger tax liabilities could still be pursued. The Bombay High Court had held that Section 87 does not authorise issuance of an SCN to an entity which had already ceased to exist following amalgamation.

🔹 ❌⚖️ Proceedings void from inception: The Bombay High Court had held that the SCN issued to the non-existent company was without jurisdiction and invalid from the beginning. With the Supreme Court dismissing the Centre’s appeal, that relief remains undisturbed.

📌 BIG LEGAL TAKEAWAY:
🏛️ A past tax liability may survive a merger, but proceedings cannot simply be initiated by issuing the statutory notice in the name of an entity that has already ceased to exist. The identity of the noticee goes to the very jurisdiction and validity of the proceedings. ⚖️🛡️

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

The AO missed the deadline to pass the Order Giving Effect (OGE).
Years later, a penalty order was still passed.

Can a penalty survive when the underlying assessment itself has failed to survive?

The Bombay HC said No.

The CIT(A) had changed the basis of taxation and directed the AO to give effect to its order.

But the AO did not pass the OGE within the prescribed time  and never passed it even thereafter.

Yet, the penalty proceedings continued, and a penalty order was eventually passed

The Court held that the assessment proceedings had abated because the OGE was not passed within the limitation period.

And if the assessment itself could no longer survive, the penalty based on that assessment could not survive either.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

DUE DILIGENCE

3) Turn site visit voice notes into structured DD reports

Here’s another immediate winner. Ever leave a site walk, sit down at your desk, stare at half a page of scribbled notes and some janky iPhone photos and realize you lost 80% of what you just saw? No more.

Lots of ways to work this into your process, but here’s an easy one.

After the walk, go sit in your car and verbally brain dump everything you can remember into Claude. Just hit the voice record button and it will transcribe to text.

Next, copy the text into a new chat with the following prompt:

Organize this site visit transcript into a structured DD report. Categorize findings by roof, envelope, plumbing, electrical, HVAC, elevator, life safety, structural, and interior/common areas. For each category, summarize condition, flag urgency (immediate / Year 1 / defer), include estimated costs if discussed, and note where a vendor bid is still needed. List any categories not covered.

Distribute to your partners and they immediate know what you know.

Next steps: Record vendor feedback on site, drop third party reports into a running DD chat, there are dozens of ways to use Claude for DD but this simple brain dump exercise is the way to start.

4. Read any third-party report in plain English

Our latest SRA report was 67 pages. The PCA was 113. The ESA was 387.

Claude is good enough now to pick up the most important elements of these reports and call them out, summarize and explain in plan English. By all means double check the work, but this will save you a tremendous amount of time.

PROMPT: Summarize this report in plain English for an underwriting audience. What are the key findings, what would worry a lender, what capex should I add to my model, and what DD action items should go on my follow-up list? Flag anything that could move      pricing.

Next steps: Drop in any PDF, ask the same thing. Earnings reports and transcripts, SEC filings, OMs, market studies, etc.

Bonus Prompt for work order reports: Review this work order history and tell me what systemic issues the building has. Call out turnover patterns by unit, recurring maintenance categories, emergency response time red flags, and anything that points to deferred capex. Be underwriting-focused, not descriptive.

DATA/TREND ANALYSIS

5) Crunch any dataset

As a data hobbyist / nerd, this one also hooked me.

Claude runs code beneath what we all see, so as long as we ask the right questions, the math is (usually) right and Excel charts are a thing of the past.

Try this: Navigate to ApartmentList. com’s data page and download their nationwide rent estimates. Upload the CSV to Claude and ask the following:

Analyze rent trends for Austin, Houston, Dallas and San Antonio, normalizing data from 2020-2026, 2022-2026, 2024-2026 and for the past 12 months.

Pick any city you want, any time period. Immediate market insights.

I find these side by side city comparisons a super helpful way to see how certain factors (Covid, immigration, etc) impact cities differently. I can now choose any combo, for any time period with a simple text prompt.

Next steps: dump your expensive, janky CoStar data in and let Claude make sense of it.

--

If you got this far, you’re well on your way. Now, here are three tips for general Claude usage I figured out the hard way (ie trial and error).

1) Ask Claude to help

This is actually tips 1-100, it totally unlocked my Claude usage.

It turns out Claude is much better at using itself than you are, so ask it how. “I want you to help me underwrite deals without losing my personal touch, how can we work together?” “I need to collect rental comp data without breaking any laws – how can you help?”

Rather than trying to brute force Claude into following your low-brow human instructions, get Claude to write the prompts, write the instructions, create you a step-by-step guide.

Embrace the fact that this is, for our purposes, the smartest thing you’ll ever come in contact with – so use the hell out of it.

2) Use Projects for work you do more than once

A Project is a workspace where Claude can more easily do the same thing over and over again.

Projects accrue memory so it doesn't lose the script, and you can even have Claude write itself instructions to perform better and create (for example) due diligence reports in the same format every time.

I have projects for: Deal underwriting, rental comp      collection, portfolio analysis, due diligence and others.

For now, don’t worry too much about whether to use      Chat or CoWork – you’ll figure that out in time and you can move projects and chats back and forth between the two.

3) Promote good outputs back into your project knowledge

An early frustration of mine was that Claude’s output      was inconsistent. I’d ask for a DD report and the categories would be different every time, the graphs looked different, etc. This is an easy fix.

Grind through with Claude what you want the output to look like - remember you can relentless correct and improve and Claude  will just happily chug along like the good little sycophant it is and keep making the report better.

Once you have the format you like, save it and upload      it back into the project main page and ask Claude to add the report to its memory so whenever you ask for “DD report” you get the same thing.

There are more advanced and cleaner ways to do this      with Skills, etc but this is an easy start.

Basic English 的概念很好，但我认为它的最佳应用不是用来背单词，而是要求 AI 使用 Basic English words 与我们对话。

比如我把Longman 3000 词交给ChatGPT，要求 AI 必须使用这个列表里的单词进行回复。我每天都和 AI 进行大量对话，而且是全英文交流，ai使用的单词全都在我的词汇舒适区，我可以不怎么费力地读懂内容，从而坚持下去。

一段时间过后，我阅读这些英文的速度就跟中文差不多了，然后再扩充词汇列表，逐渐由浅入深。整个过程不痛苦，但是我的英文水平实现了质的飞跃。

这个方法唯一的门槛就是你必须有一定的英文基础，掌握最起码的英文词汇，你要是初中水平都达不到，那可能就比较难了。

推荐操作：

在 ChatGPT 里新建一个 Project，取名为 Simple English GPT。

然后把核心词汇上传到 Project 作为数据源，再撰写 Project 的提示词，要求 GPT 只使用列表里的词汇进行回复。

text:
This intern 6x'd her company's website traffic with an AI content machine called BlogEO. 

The big f*cking problem
- Blog had almost no real measurement
- Insights lived in ~5 places (GSC, Semrush, PostHog, Sanity, prior run snapshots) so nobody joined the data
- ~70% of traffic came from 14 posts; ~50% from just 5
- Top SEO posts were often invisible to LLMs (AEO gap)

Step 1: Run the AI audit
- Pulls those five sources into one view
- Content hygiene scan first: broken links, positioning drift, deprecated products
- Broken-link fixes use @browserbase's fetch API to find the right replacement
- Broken links + missing SEO fields can auto-publish (no human gate)
- Scores every post into a ranking / opportunity queue
- Flags the top ~15 for deeper fact-check + SEO verification
- Drafts surgical edits (small, intentional) and stores each suggestion
- Edits stay small on purpose. Most posts were handwritten; don’t paste AI voice over human voice
- High-leverage changes: SEO title, meta description, swap a link
- 28-day cooldown after changes so GSC has time to catch up (no thrashing the same post)

Step 1b: Score post opportunities
• Unit of opportunity = clicks
• Click recovery: if clicks fell hard vs the last ~28 days, that lost volume is opportunity. Real click loss beats any estimate and jumps the queue.
• CTR gap: compare your CTR at a given position to what page-one / peers get at that same spot. Gap × impressions ≈ clicks you’re leaving on the table. (Alex’s example: position 9 averages ~5% CTR; you’re at 1% → the 4-pt delta is the opportunity.)
• Rank upside: if you’re on page 2/3, estimate clicks if you moved to page 1 / to the average for that better position. (Her example: post at 9.4 with a pink-dot underperform → ~7,400 click opportunity if it hit the average for that position.)
• Queue, then spend: every post gets a cheap score; only the top ~15 get the expensive fact-check / deep SEO pass (token control). Near-invisible / irrelevant queries don’t score high on purpose.

Step 3: Avoid AI slop
- New posts aren’t a firehose ideas surface as drafts, ~once a week
- Ignore / skip is a first-class option if the query isn’t worth owning
- Quality gate before anything ships
- Slack card shows who approved and who published — accountability stays with a person
- Human pride > “we shipped another AI blog”

 Step 4: Run the full blog machine
- Weekly cadence in Slack: Monday = content generation, Tuesday = audit (plus on-demand “audit this page now”)
- Agent (BB) has skills: audit, strategy, writing, generate...always drafts suggestions first
- Agent has no write path to live content until a human clicks
- Slack cards: Approve / Edit / Skip / Discard → only then does it hit the CMS
- Approved edits + outcomes land in internal DBs (including what never shipped)
- Near-miss queries (show up in search, no targeted page) feed the generator side

The results
Search impressions: +5.8x
Page-one queries: +9.8x
Avg blog position: page 2 → page 1

The Silent Emergency: Eleven Years Under the Shadow of Control

India, the land of a billion vibrant voices, is grappling with a chilling silence. For eleven years under the PM, we've witnessed an

"Undeclared Emergency@11"

—no declared curfews, no tanks, but a steady erosion of our democratic freedoms. This is the story of a Nation fighting for its soul, where the cost of speaking out grows heavier daily.

The Press in Chains
Our Fourth Estate, once a beacon of truth, now falters under relentless pressure. V-Dem and Freedom House 2025 reports label India an “electoral autocracy,” ranked “partly free.” The Press Freedom Index places us at 159/176, near Somalia’s shadow. Honest journalists face arrests, raids, and intimidation for daring to question. Laws like UAPA and sedition are weaponized, branding critics “terrorists” without trial. Media houses face raids, their voices stifled. Modi’s 11-year tenure without a single press conference speaks volumes—hate speech thrives, but truth is jailed.

Homes Turned to Rubble
Bulldozers roar across India, not for progress but as tools of vengeance. Homes, often of minorities or dissenters, are demolished in displays of state power. Families stand amid rubble, targeted for their identity or beliefs. Ministers spewing hate are rewarded, while citizens live in fear. This isn’t the India we fought for.

The Digital Gag
In the age of X, FB, Insta, and YouTube, where voices once soared, dissent is now caged. Content creators and tweeters face arrests for “misinformation” or “inciting unrest.” Over 20,000 independent voices have been silenced, their crime often a post challenging the regime. This is a democracy where keyboards are as dangerous as megaphones.

Opposition Under Siege
The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has become a weapon to intimidate opposition leaders, with raids targeting those who refuse to bow to the BJP. Homes and offices of opposition figures are stormed, cases piled up to coerce them into joining the ruling party or face relentless harassment. This blatant misuse of agencies undermines democracy, turning dissent into a dangerous act.

Puppet Election Commission
The Election Commission, once a pillar of democratic integrity, now dances to the tune of the BJP. The removal of the Chief Justice of India from the selection committee for appointing Election Commissioners has raised alarms about its independence. This move, critics argue, ensures a pliable EC, ready to tilt the electoral scales. Free and fair elections, the heartbeat of democracy, now pulse under the shadow of control.

The Leader’s Shadow
Modi’s image dominates—billboards, screens, even vaccine certificates and rail tickets. Supporters call it leadership; we see a cult stifling dissent. Parliament weakened, constitutional bodies eroded, divisive figures glorified—this is a five-fold assault on our democracy. BJP invokes 1975’s Emergency to deflect, but today’s control needs no formal name. It’s a slow, silent strangulation of our freedoms.

Nation’s Resolve
Fifty years ago, India resisted the 1975 Emergency. Today, the shackles are subtler but real. Jailed journalists, bulldozed homes, silenced voices, ED raids on opposition leaders, and a compromised Election Commission tell of a democracy under siege. As Modi marks “Samvidhan Hatya Diwas,” we say the real threat to our Constitution is now—unnamed, insidious, but ever-present.

India stands at a crossroads. Will we reclaim our chorus of voices or let silence prevail? The fight for our democracy lies in the courage of those who speak, write, and dream of a free tomorrow.

*Elon Musk’s Starlink was trying to beat Jio in India*

*But Jio used its 1st mover’s advantage to stop them in their tracks*

*The SHOCKER? Indian Gov is changing a 138 year old law that will bring Starlink back in the game*

*Here’s how Elon is rethinking internet & can possibly kill Jio:*

In 2016, when most of us were witnessing a business disruption standing in queues to get our hands on the free Jio sim card,

12,869 miles away at Rocket Road, California, a group of engineers were planning a technological disruption.

Their goal? Rethink internet access.

Their solution? Satellite Internet.

Traditionally, we have been using internet that relies on cable wires, fiber optic lines, or cellular networks.

But making cable wires or fiber optic lines available in remote villages and hard terrains is not only costly but highly impractical as well.

And this is where satellite internet and Starlink by Elon Musk comes in.

Satellite Internet uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth.

And Starlink is a collection of thousands of small satellites orbiting around 350 miles above the Earth.

For the satellite internet to work, the user on the ground connects to the Starlink dish, known as the user terminal.

The user terminal communicates with nearby Starlink satellites and forms a link to the larger Starlink network

The satellites then form a mesh network, that allows them to pass data between each other and create global network coverage.

Starlink’s motto is — ‘virtually anywhere on earth without wires or cellphone towers.’

It started its operation in 2019 and true to its motto, it’s already available in over 65 countries,

— covering all 7 continents (including Antarctica!)

But Starlink hasn’t been able to make any progress in India.

Last year, it registered its business in India via a local unit Starlink Satellite Communications Pvt Ltd.

The company had planned to provide fast internet data in the Indian market at a subsidized price compared to the international market.

It had received 5,000+ pre-orders.

But the government said Starlink Internet Services doesn’t have the license to offer services in India.

And it asked Starlink to return people’s money.

Now, one company’s loss is another company’s gain.

In Feb this year, Reliance Jio partnered up with Luxembourg-based SES to provide satellite-based broadband services in India.

And created a joint venture called — Jio Space Technology Ltd.

Moreover, Starlink and Jio Space aren’t the only contenders for India’s space spectrum.

OneWeb is backed by Airtel in India and Hughes Communication.

Tata group entity Nelco partnered up with Canada's Telesat.

And Amazon’s Kuiper is going to launch satellites in 2024.

But why are so many companies vying for India’s space spectrum?

India has a population of 1.4 billion out of which 40% do not have internet access because they are in rural and remote areas.

And traditional terrestrial networks are not easy to install.

Hence, India’s satellite broadband service is expected to reach $1.9 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 36%.

Now, because India has so many contenders for its spectrum, the question arises — who should get it?

Starlink and OneWeb wanted the government to assign licenses to companies, since spectrum is a natural resource that should be shared by companies.

But Jio wanted the government to auction the spectrum like it did with 4G & 5G 👀

Finally, the government brought in some reforms and firstly dedicated a sole agency IN-SPACe to authorize space activities for both government and private satellite communication companies.

And a bill has been proposed to replace the 138-year-old Indian Telegraph Act that currently governs the telecommunication sector.

So now, both Jio Space & OneWeb have received their GMPCS license from the Department of Telecommunications in India.

And Starlink is 3rd in line to receive the GMPCS license.

I knew Singapore was authoritarian, but I had no idea their press freedom was THIS bad. 

The World Press Freedom Index ranks 180 countries, and Singapore is in the bottom third at #123. Yikes.

For comparison, even Thailand (where I live) ranks higher at #92. So why does Singapore score worse than Thailand? Because the government of Singapore holds an extremely tight grip on local media. There are only two big media companies in the country, and both have close ties to the government. Singaporean journalists are sometimes jailed. And a culture of self-censorship isn’t helping either.

Meanwhile, here in Thailand, some journalists face censorship and lawsuits, but at least there are tons of different media outlets. The Thai media landscape is very fragmented, which is good for getting everyone’s voice heard. And there are many independent journalists critical of the government. I respect Thailand for allowing this, or at least more than a rich country like Singapore does.

Bonus: The Netherlands, where I grew up, ranks #2 on the list. I’m libertarian-minded, but I admit that the reporting of Dutch government media is just insanely good. No wonder Dutch people are well informed.

Second bonus: Iran, where I was born, ranks #177. Disgusting.

It has become fashionable these days to abuse IITs and their faculties. I get it, freedom of speech, healthy skepticism of institutions, all fair game. 

But before that fashionable takedown becomes the whole story, sit with this 1 fact for a second....

Right now, last month, IIT profs have put more free, peer-reviewed, university grade course content into the world than any other institution on the planet, and most Indians have never watched a single hour of it.

2001....

A handful of IIT directors come back from a trip to Carnegie Mellon, having seen an American prof build an entire functioning university around teaching people online. 

They are stunned enough to try replicating it for India, in engineering, at a scale nobody had attempted before.

The idea finally took shape under Atal Bihari Vajpayee's government. The man holding the HRD portfolio through that entire stretch, 1998-2004, was Murli Manohar Joshi, himself a physics prof before he was ever a minister. 

On January 26, 2003, months before NPTEL's own official rollout that year, Joshi Ji personally inaugurated a companion initiative, the Eklavya Technology Channel, explicitly built to beam actual IIT classrooms into homes across the country. 

7 IITs and the IISc quietly went live. 

No press conference most people remember. Just profs, cameras, and a govt that wrote the check for something nobody could fully prove would work.

The word "MOOC" did not even exist yet. Coursera and edX launched in 2012. 

The term was not even coined until 2008. NPTEL was already recording real lectures years before Silicon Valley invented free online university education and got magazine covers for it. 

India did not copy the MOOC revolution, it built one of the first drafts before anyone had a name for it.

Fast forward to now. 

NPTEL is the largest repository of engineering and science course content on Earth: 

- 56,000+ hours of lectures

-3,200+ courses

- a YouTube channel with 1.86B views and 5.6M subscribers

...built entirely by government-funded faculty, not a venture-backed edtech company. 

Not entertainment.... 

Thermodynamics. Signal processing. Soil mechanics. Quantum Mechanics. 

Built by profs people love to mock as "out of touch," "irrelevant," "stuck in an old system."

A student in rural Bihar with a smartphone has, right now, the same lecture an IIT KGP student sat through, free, no JEE rank required. 

And yet ask most students outside the IIT system if they have done a single NPTEL certification, and you will mostly get silence. 

Employers still do not weight it the way they weight a foreign MOOC certificate with a fraction of the rigor. The exact students this was built for often do not know it exists.

If a country builds the largest free reservoir of elite education on the planet, a decade ahead of everyone else, and barely drinks from it, is that the institution's failure / ours, for criticizing loudly and never once checking what is already free and sitting right there?

Criticize the IITs all you want, no institution should be above scrutiny. But this particular story deserves the same volume as the criticism. It just never gets it.

@TeamYouTube this situation has gone way beyond a normal enforcement issue. On July 28, my channel started receiving an unusual wave of privacy complaints. Within roughly 3 days, 40+ complaints were filed against 41 completely unrelated videos, and 31 videos were removed. I appealed multiple removals and repeatedly contacted YouTube Support and Legal, but I never received a clear, case-specific explanation of the alleged privacy violations.

Then on August 14, the entire channel was terminated for Impersonation. I appealed and was rejected. When I contacted Creator Support, I was first told the termination was for Spam, despite the termination notice clearly stating Impersonation. The case was escalated, and I was then told the internal review confirmed Impersonation. I repeatedly asked a simple question: Who or what did I supposedly impersonate, and what exactly on the channel violated the policy? No specific answer was provided.

I submitted another official appeal through Google Form. It was confirmed as received and sent for specialized review, but that appeal has now also been rejected for Impersonation.

So after multiple reviews, I still haven't been told what specific person, channel, branding, video, or conduct supposedly constituted impersonation. I have never intentionally impersonated anyone or claimed to represent another creator or entity.

The matter is now pending before GAC in India and has also been brought to @SFLCin.

I am not asking for special treatment. I am asking for a fair, evidence-based review and a clear explanation of what actually happened. Please escalate this properly and reconsider the termination. @YouTube @UpdatesFromYT @YouTubeCreators @YouTubeIndia

Ray-Ban Meta glasses struck again. A woman walking home alone was secretly recorded by a man who approached her, then posted the footage on Instagram alongside similar clips of him doing this to other women, as part of "pickup" content.

She's filed a police complaint for stalking and voyeurism. IFF is assisting her with a legal notice to the creator, Instagram, and Meta, the second such notice against Meta in India.

This isn't a one off. It's a design problem.
Read more about it: https://t.co/x5Gzp2NFF0

A woman was followed, stopped on a dark street, secretly recorded through Ray-Ban Meta glasses and turned into an Instagram “pickup” reel that reached over 23 lakh views. Now, our legal notice seeks accountability from both him and Meta. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/x5Gzp2NFF0

The legal notice therefore puts Meta on notice not merely as the platform hosting the video, but as the designer, developer, manufacturer, marketer and seller of the glasses. It alleges negligence and product liability, arguing that Meta knew about the pattern of misuse but continued selling the device without an effective way for non-users or people being recorded to report that misuse. (9/10)

The notice seeks removal of every copy, preservation and disclosure of evidence, suspension of monetisation, an account of profits, an apology, and ₹2.05 crore in compensatory and exemplary damages. This case raises a larger question: when a company makes a camera that can be worn like ordinary glasses, who protects the person being recorded? Privacy cannot depend on whether the person being filmed has an Instagram account. (10/10)

The Supreme Court has closed India's Got Latent cases, but the question of an “Influencer Code” is not entirely over. On 14 August 2026, the Court quashed all FIRs arising from the episode and left the “larger issues” of regulating online speech for “another appropriate case”. Here is what that means. (1/7)

Read More: https://t.co/hecp2rl9W4

That qualifier matters. Executive action restricting speech must have a legal basis consistent with Article 19. The Court has previously held that executive instructions cannot independently impose restrictions on fundamental rights. The signed order also contains no finding that the content in question was obscene, nor does it establish a new standard for online speech. (6/7)

For now, there are no guidelines and no pending judicial direction requiring them. But MIB can still attempt regulatory changes, including through amendments to the IT Rules. If it does, IFF will insist on the public consultation promised to the Supreme Court, compliance with the Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy and meaningful participation by affected creators and users. (7/7)

NIXI has changed its justification for suspending chalosansad dot in yet again. After first citing a “critical keyword”, and then relying on a 2004 policy clause that did not apply, it now invokes the Emblems Act and demands Central Government permission within seven days. On 8 September, IFF wrote back seeking a standstill and answers. (1/7)
Read More: https://t.co/2grOxR1bMy

The timing matters. The domain was suspended on 22 July. NIXI’s new legal opinion was obtained on 29 August, more than a month later and only after we challenged its earlier reasons. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that administrative action must stand or fall on the reasons given when the decision was made; authorities cannot ordinarily supplement an order with new reasons after it is challenged. (6/7)

NIXI has now also said that six other .in domains containing “Sansad”, along with other domains containing “Sansad”, “Parliament” or cognate expressions, will be examined. On 8 September, we asked NIXI for a 48-hour standstill on de-registration, deletion, transfer or reallocation of chalosansad dot in, confirmation of Aadhaar deletion, and disclosure of the correspondence it says raised concerns about publication. If no standstill is given, the registrant will approach the court. (7/7)

Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX

NIXI has also given the registrant seven days to produce Central Government permission. Yet its reply identifies no ministry, officer, form, fee, procedure or timeline through which such permission can actually be obtained. We have therefore asked NIXI to explain the legal basis for this demand, and to provide the legal opinion dated 29 August on which its new position relies. (5/7)

quotedTweet.text:
On September 10th, 2013, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act, a vague law that was being used to arrest people for simply expressing dissent online.

11 years later, Maharashtra wants to bring it back in a new form, by amending the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for "online criminal defamation." But defamation is already covered under Section 356 of the BNS, and civil remedies already exist.

So why does the police need this new power? Recent FIRs against citizens and influencers for calling out potholes and infrastructure failures may hold the answer. We've fought this battle before. We don't need a new 66A with a new number.

text:
A 2:01-minute reel documenting villagers’ concerns over the proposed Google data centre in Visakhapatnam was blocked in India for 111 days. On 10 September 2026, it quietly came back online. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/TVxhdw9ZA1

The Sahyog route also raises a serious constitutional concern. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because the blocking framework contained procedural safeguards, including notice, hearing and a reasoned order. Section 79(3)(b), meanwhile, was read down to require a court order or government notification. A system that blocks first and explains nothing is difficult to reconcile with those safeguards. (9/10)

The reel is back, and we welcome that. But the questions remain unanswered, Who ordered the blocking? Why did the order name an unrelated person? Was a periodic review conducted? Why was the reel restored? IFF will continue seeking these answers from Andhra Pradesh authorities. Journalists should not need months of litigation to learn why their public-interest reporting was censored. (10/10)
